newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco talks resume as jury deliberates.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco talks resume as jury deliberates.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

A Florida jury's deliberations in a widely watched tobacco case are boosting the pressure on cigarette makers as they resume negotiations Monday with state attorneys general aimed at resolving growing litigation.

The threat of a possible verdict against the industry after the recent court ruling upholding the Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate tobacco as a drug has raised the stakes in the talks, prompting cigarette makers to agree to a number of concessions.

If a settlement can be reached, the industry would stop billboard advertising, end vending machine sales and finance anti-smoking programmes, according to published reports. USA Today reported Monday that cigarette makers would also accept workplace bans on smoking and stricter package warning labels.

In making such concessions, the industry hopes to settle some of the suits against it or at least cap its liability. But state officials have grown insistent that a settlement exclude blanket immunity so total protection from lawsuits does not seem to be an option for cigarette makers.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore was asked by reporters before he went into a meeting of attorneys general, public health and plaintiffs' lawyers, whether the tobacco industry had given up on the idea of total immunity.
"These guys don't give up on anything, but we're making progress on that issue," he said.

Richard Scruggs, a Mississippi lawyer who is assisting the state in its litigation, said the attorneys general had swapped ideas on the liability issue with industry officials in recent days. The parties were to meet on Monday afternoon.
Moore said they expected to discuss public health issues and liability at the meeting.

On Monday, Montana became the 25th state to sue cigarette makers to recover the health care costs of treating smokers, and three more were expected to file suit shortly. Moore said that 28 states were involved in the negotiations.

The first of the state trials is scheduled for July in Mississippi. The industry also faces hundreds of individual suits filed by smokers and their families including the current Florida trial as well as a number of class actions.

The industry, which began negotiating directly with the attorneys general early last month, has been dealt several big blows recently. The most damaging was last month's ruling by a Greensboro, N.C., federal judge, who once represented tobacco growers as a private attorney, that held the FDA has the power to regulate tobacco.

Although the judge said the FDA did not have the authority to regulate advertising of cigarettes, the Supreme Court refused a few days later to hear a challenge to a Baltimore law restricting placement of tobacco billboards.

Legal experts predicted the move would strengthen efforts by cities and towns to restrict tobacco ads and just last week a proposal was made in New York City to ban tobacco billboards and promotions near schools and other locations where children gather. Washington State's King County, which encompasses Seattle, is expected to vote on a similar proposal on May 30.

While these losses have pressured cigarette makers to try to find a solution soon, some industry critics believe the defeats make a settlement premature or even unnecessary. Some health groups in particular have opposed an accord.
Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey even wrote his colleagues last Friday urging them against acting too hastily.

"Is this the right time to settle?" he wrote. "Frankly, it may not be. We have strong cases and if we try and win even a few, we will have brought the industry not just to the table, but to its knees."

Even as the industry and attorneys general resume their talks, the Jacksonville, Fla., jury was deliberating whether R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings, could be held liable for a smoker's death.

The case is being widely watched because one of the plaintiff's lawyers is Norwood "Woody" Wilner, who won a verdict against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. last summer, which sent tobacco companies' stocks plunging. If he wins again, many legal experts say that will mean public opinion is turning against the industry, which for years won almost every case.
Even if the industry is not held liable in the Jacksonville trial, Wilner has filed about 300 other cases and the odds are that he would probably win some of the other suits.
